paragraphs.text: Tikopia is one of the smallest and most remote islands in the South Pacific—a region where neither characteristic is unusual. Just three kilometres long and supporting a 1,200-strong Polynesian population, there is no harbour or airport, no telephones, shops or hotels. Although originally uninhabited, Tikopia has a long human history, which is still being unraveled. Fragments of pottery unearthed by archaeologists indicate that the first visitors were Polynesian explorers who arrived around 2,000 years ago, but that no permanent settlement was made until the ancestors of the present Tikopians reached the island around the 7th century AD.

Because of its tiny size and extreme isolation, Tikopia has had very little contact with the outside world – and for these exact same reasons, anthropologists have long considered it their most desired destination in the South Pacific. Here and here alone, it is possible to study a traditional Polynesian culture which has changed little for hundreds of years. The most influential of the many scientists who have worked on Tikopia was Professor Raymond Firth, whose pioneering methodology involved living among the Islanders, perhaps for years at a time, adopting their lifestyle and learning their language so as to observe their culture as an “insider.” The resulting data were infinitely more detailed than any previously gathered, and were based exclusively on Tikopia, although Firth was the first to admit his lengthy sojourns on the island resulted partly from the difficulties of organising a ship to pick him up from such a remote place.

One aspect of Tikopian life which Firth studied was the art of tattooing, a cultural institution in all Polynesian societies. Tattoos were thought to beautify the body and contribute to social cohesion. In the Tikopian language they are called te tau and a similar term is used throughout the thousands of Pacific Islands, whose languages are closely related. When European sailors first arrived in the Pacific, they adopted these skin decorations themselves, though they misheard the local name and called them tattoos. The sailors then carried the art of tattooing across the oceans and today, in some parts of the world, young people consider tattoos the height of fashion.

Modern tattoos in places like America and Europe are made with machines and ink but on Tikopia all the equipment used must be made from naturally occurring resources. Essentially, two items are required. Pigment is the dye used to stain the skin a black colour, and it is made of the sap from inside the vola tree, a liquid which hardens once it is exposed to the air to form balls. These are subsequently heated on a fire laid in a shallow hole. The fire consists of only smouldering embers because the sap is placed in a coconut shell, which will be destroyed if the fire is too hot. As the sap burns it gives off soot, which settles on a stone above the fire. Once the soot is scraped off and mixed with sea water it is ready for use.

The other item is a ‘chisel’, used to push the pigment into the skin. The blade is fabricated from the wing bone of a seabird – the kotoko is preferred, as those of the frigate bird are too fragile and tend to break off. This is attached to a long, thin handle, which must be sufficiently heavy to give the tool momentum, so the heartwood of a bush called te ora is chosen to meet this requirement. The two are bound together using tau tree bark torn into strips.

Most adult Tikopians wear tattoos and there are strict rules laid down by custom dictating the designs that may appear on various parts of the body. Some men’s tattoos reflect the islander’s spiritual links with the vast ocean that dominates their lives, while women’s tattoos are considered more decorative. Men’s facial tattoos are worn by all age groups and consist of small fish shapes. From one to seven may be placed vertically, head downwards, on the forehead. While at the corner of the eye there is usually a single horizontal fish always facing inwards so it appears to be swimming towards the centre-line of the face. Women rarely wear fish shapes on their faces because fishing is a man’s job on the island. Usually they have bare foreheads and wear the image of a bird at the corner of the eye. But the most common women’s tattoo, just worn by mothers, commences on the chin, below the bottom lip, and extends up the jaw bone as far as the earlobe.

The large pattern which covers the chests of men on Tikopia is the most spiritually significant of all the island’s tattoo designs, for within lie the body’s vital organs, the heart and lungs, so the exterior surface is covered with the most time-consuming and precious tattoos. Only older men will be marked with a full chest tattoo. The most common shapes are triangles, which are arranged on a grid of vertical and horizontal lines. Almost as common are the back tattoos worn by middle-aged men. The entire back is covered by vertical lines beginning just below the shoulder blades and terminating at the waistline. The verticals are decorated with short cross lines at intervals of about 100 mm and symbolize te rou mei – sticks of great length – which Tikopian men use to pick the fruit out of the huge breadfruit trees, which, together with fish, form the staples of the Islanders’ diet.
